subject: logistic regression with spatial auto-covariate and missing data imputation

messages.author: 839eb4092a42aa65
messages.subject: logistic regression with spatial auto-covariate and missing data imputation
parts:
Hi all,

I'm trying to fit a logistic regression to some simulated data, and I'm having trouble retrieving parameter estimates that approximate those that were used to generate the data and was wondering if anyone had any ideas on why this might be.

The model includes a single predictor variable (bounded between 0-1), a spatial auto-covariate, and requires some missing data to be imputed to estimate some of the spatial auto-covariates.

The data was simulated with the following back-story in mind:

The goal of the study is to determine the effect of FPC (foliage projective cover (%)) on distribution of a species in the study area. The square study area was divided up into grid cells of equal sizes.
Observers were sent out to most of the grid cells, and the species was recorded as being present (1) or absent (0) in these grid cells. These observations are assumed to contain no false-positives or false-negatives. However due to finite resources, some grid cells were not visited and the presence or absence of the species in these grid cells is unknown.

This species is known to have a strongly spatially auto-correlated distribution, and so this will be taken into account using a spatial auto-covariate. The spatial-autocovariate for a given cell is the average occupancy in its neighboring cells (max. 8). In order to calculate the spatial auto-covariate for cells that are neighbors with cells that were not visited, the probability of the species occupying the cells that were not visited must be imputed in the model.

I've attached the R script that generates the data, runs my best attempt at the model, and includes my sessionInfo() in the comments (autocovariate_example.txt), the data dump file (autocov_data.txt), and the stan model (autocov_model.txt). The R script is heavily commented so may offer additional context.

Thank you, Jeff

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] logistic regression with spatial auto-covariate and missing data imputation
parts:
Hi, Jeff.  Just speaking generically, one way to check this sort of fake-data simulation is to draw the parameters from the prior.  Then the posterior coverage should be exact (up to computational accuracy).  For details, you can take a look at the 2006 paper by Cook, Gelman, and Rubin (at my website linked from the published papers page).  It's worth checking, as there can be various reasons (even possibly a Stan bug!) that is causing your problem.
I hope this helps.
Andrew

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] logistic regression with spatial auto-covariate and missing data imputation
parts:
Did you try building this up from first building a model
without missing data and verifying that it could fit the data?
Then you should have at least the likelihood and priors down.

Also, if you haven't tried it already, I'd also suggest using
some intermediate print statements to make sure all the intermediate
calculations are happening the way you want them to.

(For both of these issues, what we really need is some way to define
and test subprograms in a modular way.)

You might also consider using a Gaussian process logistic regression
model if the number of data points isn't too high --- it seems to have
most of the features you're after built into its basic
structure.

Depending on the kind of problem you're having with fitting,
you might want to choose slightly more informative priors:

intercept ~ normal(0,1000);
fpc_slope ~ normal(0,1000);
auto_slope ~ normal(0,1000);
sigma_miss ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);

If the data highly underdetermines a variable with a very fat
prior, it can drag the whole model around with it. So I'd want
to see what these variables were doing.

As a minor point, I'd define data items like this:

int numTotalPlus1; // number of grid cells total + 1

as transformed data to make sure they're always right.

If you actually lay the data out
on a grid, you should also be able to calculate quantities
like numNeighbors directly in Stan.

Are statements like these:

for (currNeighPos in 1:8) {
currAutoVal<-currAutoVal+Y_total_est[Y_neighMat[missPos[currPos3],currNeighPos]];
}

appropriately accounting for the edge cases?

Spatially, aren't corner connections different than edge ones?

A B C
D . E
F G H

It seems B/D/E/G should have more effect on the center
than A/C/F/H because of distance. This is again something the Gaussian
process should do automatically.

- Bob
